readerTitle: $240 once or $15 a month: which one earns more?
caseNote: 가상 사례 (로봇청소기 매장, 사내 데이터 분석팀) + 실제 기업 (Adobe, softwareNote) · 매장·사내팀 수치는 모두 설명용
insight: 구독 가격표의 크기가 아니라 고객이 머무는 기간이 구독의 가치를 정한다. 구독은 매달 다시 벌어야 하는 약속이다.
misconception: 월 구독은 계속 들어오는 돈이므로 언제나 일시불 판매보다 고객당 매출이 많다.

sources.text: 구독 경제의 표준 개념 (평균 유지 기간 ≈ 1 ÷ 월 해지율, 고객 생애 매출)
Adobe, Creative Cloud 전환 발표 (2013년 5월, Creative Suite 신규 판매 중단)

factChecks.note: 평균 유지 기간 = 1 ÷ 월 해지율은 매달 같은 비율로 해지한다는 단순화된 가정입니다. 실제로는 초기 해지가 더 많습니다. 카드에 "roughly"로 표기했습니다.
Adobe가 2013년 Creative Suite 신규 버전 판매를 멈추고 Creative Cloud 구독으로 전환했다는 내용은 게시 전 Adobe 공식 발표로 다시 확인하세요. 매출 수치는 쓰지 않았습니다.

cards.title: $240 once or $15 a month: which one earns more?
body: Two price tags for the same robot vacuum. Buy it today for $240. Or take a plan for $15 a month, with parts and repairs included.
The monthly plan seems to win easily. After two years it brings in $360. But that answer hides an assumption about customers.

image.label: One robot vacuum with two price tags: $240 and $15/month
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 매장 진열대 위 로봇청소기 한 대에 가격표 두 개가 달려 있음: "$240"와 "$15/month". 월 가격표 뒤로 달력 페이지가 몇 장 넘어가다 중간에 끊긴 모습. 실제 브랜드 로고 금지.

cards.title: Which option earns more per customer?
body: You run a home-appliance store. A supplier lets you offer the vacuum either way: $240 to buy, or $15 a month to use, cancel any time.
Stores already running the plan say about 10% of subscribers cancel each month. Looking only at money in, which earns more per customer?

options.text: The plan. $15 a month passes $240 after 16 months and keeps going
options.feedback: True only if customers stay 16 months or more. The price tag tells you the rate, not how long the money keeps coming.

options.text: The one-time sale, given that cancel rate
options.feedback: Right. At 10% a month, the average customer stays about 10 months and pays about $150. The next card shows why.

options.text: They come out about even, since the plan has a lower price but runs longer
options.feedback: Good instinct to weigh price against time. But at this cancel rate the plan falls well short of $240.

cards.title: It all depends on how long they stay.
body: If a set share of customers cancels each month, the average stay is roughly **1 ÷ the cancel rate**. At 10%, that's 10 months, or $150.
The plan only beats $240 if customers stay longer than 16 months. That means fewer than about 6% cancelling each month.

image.label: It all depends on how long they stay.
image.brief: Labeled HTML chart from the lesson numbers

cards.title: Subscription vs one-time purchase
body: A **one-time purchase** sells ownership. You get the money up front, and the customer carries the risk that the product turns out not to be worth it.
A **subscription** sells continued use. The money arrives over time, and customers can leave any month. So the risk moves to you: you have to earn the payment again every month.

image.label: Lump of coins on one side, a thin stream of coins on the other
image.brief: 좌우 비교 인포그래픽. 왼쪽 "One-time": 동전 더미가 한 번에 떨어짐. 오른쪽 "Subscription": 매달 동전이 한 개씩 떨어지고, 중간중간 고객 아이콘이 문 밖으로 나감. 하단 문구 "Earn it again every month".

cards.softwareNote: In 2013, Adobe stopped selling new boxed versions of Creative Suite and moved to Creative Cloud subscriptions. A subscription like that only pays off if regular updates keep giving customers a reason to stay.

cards.title: Match the price to how the value arrives.
body: Ask when customers get value from what you sell. Then price it the same way.
list: **Value keeps coming:** supplies, upkeep, updates, ongoing service. A subscription fits.
**Value arrives once:** a sofa, a wedding cake, a finished renovation. Sell it once.
**Big upfront cost scares buyers:** a monthly plan can help, but only if they stay long enough.
cards.callout: If customers keep getting value, they keep paying. If not, they cancel.

cards.title: A subscription can drain your cash first.
body: With the one-time sale, the store collects $240 on day one. With the plan, it hands over a vacuum and collects $15. Paying for the vacuum itself gets covered slowly, over many months.
So a fast-growing subscription business can run short of cash just as it succeeds. Each new customer costs money now and pays back later.
And customers notice when they keep paying for something that never changes. That's often when they cancel.

cards.title: Now it's a team inside a company.
body: You lead an internal data team that charges other departments for its work. Building a sales dashboard takes a big effort up front. After that, keeping the data fresh takes a few hours a month.
Departments often drop dashboards within a year after reorganizations. How should you charge?

options.feedback: Easy to say yes to. But if a department keeps it 10 months, you collect $15,000 for a build that cost you far more effort.

options.text: One fee of $24,000 for the build
options.feedback: It covers the build. But the monthly upkeep becomes free work that lasts as long as they use the dashboard.

options.text: A build fee, plus a small monthly fee for upkeep
options.feedback: Each part of the price matches how the value arrives. The build gets paid once. The upkeep gets paid only while the department still uses it.

cards.title: A subscription is worth what customers stay for.
body: Compare the one-time price with the monthly price times the average stay. Then ask whether your value really keeps arriving each month.
**Try it today:** pick one thing you sell. Is its value delivered once or over time? Check whether your price follows the same pattern.
